content: Fluoride compounds, when present in high concentrations, are toxic to humans. A dose of approximately 5 grams of pure sodium fluoride is lethal for most adults, with the fatal dose estimated to be around 70 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. Acute fluoride toxicity is believed to occur at doses ranging from 2 to 8 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, with lethal doses reported at 16 milligrams per kilogram in children and 32 to 64 milligrams per kilogram in adults. Poisoning typically results from the ingestion of fluoride-containing products, whether accidental or intentional. When ingested, fluoride compounds are rapidly absorbed through the intestines. Fluoride is also sequestered in the body, with trace amounts being incorporated into bone tissue. Contact with fluoride compounds at high concentrations, whether through the skin or eyes, is hazardous. The only widely recognized adverse effect of low-concentration water fluoridation is dental fluorosis. This condition arises from excessive fluoride intake during the developmental stages of teeth, prior to their eruption into the oral cavity. Dental fluorosis can result in tooth discoloration (yellowing), hypothyroidism, or increased brittleness of bones and teeth. The term excessive in this context refers to fluoride concentrations significantly higher than the recommended levels of 0.7 to 1.2 parts per million (ppm) in fluoridated water. In small amounts, fluoride is beneficial for dental health, as seen in fluoride therapy. One of the clinical manifestations of fluoride poisoning is gastrointestinal inflammation, as fluoride has a corrosive effect on the mucous membranes lining the digestive tract. Fluoride toxicity has also been associated with metabolic disturbances, including an increased sensitivity to natural plant toxins such as salicylates. This may be particularly relevant for individuals with pre-existing salicylate intolerance, such as those with ADHD or autism spectrum disorders. Potential Sources of Fluoride Poisoning Fluoride poisoning can result from various sources, though not all have been scientifically validated. Historically, most cases have been linked to accidental ingestion of insecticides or rodenticides containing fluoride. Other potential sources include: Air pollution Anesthetics Antibiotics Automobile wheel-cleaning products Contaminated food and beverages Dietary supplements containing sodium fluoride Fluoridated milk or salt Public water fluoridation Fluoride tablets Glass-etching or chrome-cleaning agents (e.g. These conditions are more prevalent in regions where natural fluoride levels in drinking water exceed those added to public water supplies in the United States. The severity of symptoms depends on the amount of fluoride ingested. The clinical presentation suggests significant metabolic dysfunction, resembling hypothyroidism. Gastrointestinal Symptoms Abdominal pain Diarrhea Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) Excessive salivation (hypersalivation) Mucosal injury Nausea Vomiting Electrolyte Abnormalities Elevated potassium levels (hyperkalemia) Low calcium levels (hypocalcemia) Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) Low magnesium levels (hypomagnesemia) Neurological Effects Headache Hyperactive reflexes Muscle weakness Muscle spasms Tingling or numbness (paresthesia) Seizures Tetanic muscle contractions Tremors Cardiovascular Effects Cardiac arrest Shock Widened QRS complex on ECG Various arrhythmias Mechanism of Action Ingested fluoride primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract. In the stomach, it can form hydrofluoric acid, which causes irritation or corrosion of the gastrointestinal lining. The gastrointestinal system is typically the first and most significantly affected organ system following fluoride ingestion. Treatment of Fluoride Poisoning In cases of accidental ingestion, administering milk, calcium carbonate, or milk of magnesia can help slow the absorption of fluoride.
